This scenario covers both role variants as positive cases, plus negative coverage for invalid enum values and a malformed cpus[] entry not exercised by other groups.

name: Desired State — Default Negotiation and Zero-Deployment Manifest
description: Per docs.margo.org/specification/margo-management-interface/desired-state: (1) the WFM (here, our mock server) MUST default to application/vnd.margo.manifest.v1+json when the Accept header is omitted entirely, not just when it's the exact expected value; (2) when a client has zero deployments assigned, the manifest's deployments field MUST still be a valid (empty) array. Both are edge cases the other device-supplier groups don't exercise directly. Note: the spec also requires the manifest's bundle field to be explicit null (not omitted) when deployments is empty — not independently verified here, because this suite's validation engine can't distinguish a field that's present-but-null from one that's absent (both read as Go/JS nil); confirmed instead by reading the mock server's response-construction code directly.

steps.name: Get Deployments With No Accept Header — Defaults To Manifest Format
Get Deployments — Zero Deployments Still Returns A Valid (Empty) Manifest

name: MI-008 — Manifest With Unsupported Digest Algorithm Must Be Rejected
description: SUITE SELF-TEST for MARGO-DEV-MANAGEMENTINTERFACE-008 ('If a manifest references an unsupported digest algorithm, the client MUST treat the manifest as invalid and abort processing'). The mock is armed with the 'unsupported_digest_algorithm' negative fixture so GET /deployments returns a manifest whose digests use sha512 instead of sha256. The suite then asserts (a) the fixture is actually present in the response and (b) its own manifest-conformance check (expect_manifest_rejected) flags the manifest for rejection. This proves the suite would correctly fail a real device that acted on such a manifest.

steps.name: GET Deployments — Manifest Uses An Unsupported Digest Algorithm And Must Be Rejected

name: MI-006/009 — Bundle Digest That Doesn't Match Content Must Be Rejected
description: SUITE SELF-TEST for MARGO-DEV-MANAGEMENTINTERFACE-006 / -009: the client MUST verify computed digests match manifest values and abort on any mismatch. The 'bundle_digest_mismatch' fixture corrupts bundle.digest while leaving bundle.url pointing at the real archive; evaluateManifest downloads it, hashes it, and must flag the mismatch.

steps.name: GET Deployments — Bundle Digest Mismatch Must Be Rejected

name: MI-019 — Any Fetched Artifact With A Wrong Digest Must Be Rejected
description: SUITE SELF-TEST for MARGO-DEV-MANAGEMENTINTERFACE-019: the client MUST verify the digest of every fetched artifact. The 'deployment_digest_mismatch' fixture corrupts the first deployments[].digest only (the bundle digest stays correct), so the violation is caught on a per-deployment artifact, not the bundle.

steps.name: GET Deployments — Deployment Digest Mismatch Must Be Rejected

name: MI-010 — A manifestVersion Not Strictly Greater Than The Last Must Be Rejected
description: SUITE SELF-TEST for MARGO-DEV-MANAGEMENTINTERFACE-010. The scenario first reads a manifest at version >= 2 (so the runner records it), then the 'non_increasing_manifest_version' fixture serves a manifest back at version 1; evaluateManifest must reject it as a rollback.

steps.name: GET Deployments — Establish The Current Version
GET Deployments — Version Went Backwards, Must Be Rejected

name: MI-025/026 — A Wrong sizeBytes (Digest Still Valid) Must NOT Cause Rejection
description: SUITE SELF-TEST for MARGO-DEV-MANAGEMENTINTERFACE-025 / -026: sizeBytes MUST NOT be used for integrity verification. The 'wrong_size_bytes' fixture sets every sizeBytes to 1 but leaves digests correct; a conformant client verifies by digest and MUST still proceed, so the suite asserts expect_manifest_accepted.

steps.name: GET Deployments — sizeBytes Is Bogus But The Manifest Is Still Acceptable

name: MI-012 — Server Accepts An ecdsa-p384-sha384 Signed Client
description: MARGO-DEV-MANAGEMENTINTERFACE-012: implementations MUST support ecdsa-p384-sha384. The scenario signs every request with a P-384 device key (signing_key at scenario level); htmsig derives ecdsa-p384-sha384 from the curve. A successful signed GET proves the WFM verifies P-384 signatures.

steps.name: Signed GET Deployments Succeeds (P-384 signature verified)

name: MI-014 — Server Accepts An rsa-v1_5-sha256 Signed Client
description: MARGO-DEV-MANAGEMENTINTERFACE-014: implementations MUST support rsa-v1_5-sha256. The scenario signs with an RSA-2048 device key and pins signing_algorithm to rsa-v1_5-sha256 (htmsig would otherwise default RSA keys to rsa-pss-sha512). A successful signed GET proves the WFM verifies rsa-v1_5-sha256.

steps.name: Signed GET Deployments Succeeds (rsa-v1_5-sha256 signature verified)

name: MI-004 — Device Certificate Must Conform To RFC 5280
description: MARGO-DEV-MANAGEMENTINTERFACE-004: all client certificates MUST conform to RFC 5280. Positive: a normal device cert onboards (201). Negative: a cert with a 1024-bit RSA key — below the RFC 5280 / CA-Browser Forum floor — is rejected with 422. The mock's certRFC5280Violation() also checks the validity window and empty-subject/no-SAN.

steps.name: Onboard With A Conforming Certificate — Accepted
Onboard With A Weak-Key (1024-bit RSA) Certificate — Rejected

name: MI-018 — Device Trusts The WFM Server Certificate Via The Root CA
description: MARGO-DEV-MANAGEMENTINTERFACE-018: the client MUST trust the WFM's server certificate through a securely obtained root CA. verify_tls makes the runner verify the server cert against certs/ca-cert.pem (the CA a device fetches from the Certificate API). Positive: the real WFM (CA-signed cert) is trusted. Negative: the :3002 listener presents a cert NOT signed by that CA, so the connection MUST fail. Assumes a local mock (:3001 / :3002).

steps.name: GET Certificate Over A CA-Verified TLS Connection — Succeeds
Connect To A Server Whose Cert Is Not CA-Signed — Refused

name: Flexible Order — Desired State Reconciliation Lifecycle
description: Per docs.margo.org/specification/margo-management-interface/desired-state, 'desired state' is a reconciliation pattern (poll -> version check -> fetch -> reconcile -> report status), not a single endpoint — confirmed against a real device-agent's stateSync/deployment/status logs on this VM. This scenario scripts the mock server's desired-state timeline via the test-control endpoint (PUT .../test/clients/{reconClientId}/deployments, not part of the real spec) to exercise manifestVersion progression, ETag steady-state caching, and add/remove reconciliation with status reporting — mirroring the real device-agent trace (empty -> DESIRED-STATE-ADDED -> installed -> removed). Onboards its own dedicated client (not the shared {clientId}) so its hardcoded manifestVersion assertions stay valid no matter what order this scenario runs in relative to others that also mutate the shared client's desired state.

steps.name: Onboard Dedicated Client For This Scenario (not shared)
Get Deployments — Confirm Empty Desired State
Re-poll With Same ETag — Steady State (304, no reconciliation needed)
Get Deployments — Confirm Deployment Present, Version Advanced
Unassign Second Deployment (test-control) — back to default only
Report Status: removed (second deployment, no longer desired)
Get Deployments — Confirm Restored To Default Only

name: Flexible Order — Multi-App Desired State (mock server reports both apps)
description: Device-supplier counterpart to the wfm-supplier multi-app scenario, but fully deterministic since this mock server is entirely under test-harness control (no external operator to wait on). Uses the test-control endpoint to assign two REAL sample apps (sample-app-a: nginx, sample-app-b: redis — see device-supplier/sample-apps/{app-a,app-b}/compose.yaml, served by this mock server at /sample-apps/{app}/compose.yaml) simultaneously, verifies the mock server correctly reports BOTH in one desired-state manifest, brings both to 'installed' via individual status reports, then removes one (app-b) and verifies exactly one (app-a) remains. Ends by restoring the original default deployment (a3e2f5dc-912e-494f-8395-52cf3769bc06), matching every other flexible-order scenario's assumption, so this is safe to run in any shuffle order.

steps.name: Get Deployments — Confirm Mock Server Reports Both Apps
Fetch App A Deployment Manifest (nginx compose)
Fetch App A's Actual compose.yaml (served by this mock server)
Fetch App B Deployment Manifest (redis compose)
Fetch App B's Actual compose.yaml (served by this mock server)
Report App B Status: installed — both apps now running
Remove App B, Keep App A (test-control)
Get Deployments — Confirm Exactly App A Remains
Report App B Status: removed (no longer desired)
Restore Default Deployment (test-control) — leave shared client in the state siblings expect
Get Deployments — Confirm Restored To Default Only
